title: Student-Centered Distillation Narrows the Agentic Gap Between Small and Large LLMs
claim: Prior distillation has the student clone full teacher trajectories; ours lets the student explore and the teacher fixes only the earliest error.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, (a) prior vs (b) ours with dashed-border sub-stages
description: The figure has two large dashed-border panels. Panel (a), on the left, is titled 'Previous Methods: Teacher Acts, Student Clones'. It shows a teacher icon, a math word problem, and three peach-colored trajectory steps (σ1–σ3). Each step has Thought, Action (code box), and Observation. A bottom strip shows Q→σ1σ2σ3 with a dashed SFT arrow to a student icon. Panel (b), on the right, is titled 'Ours: Student Explores, Teacher Corrects'. A blue box holds the student's green trajectory with a red X on the faulty step σ2. A teacher with a magnifying glass reviews it globally and finds the first error. A second blue box shows the corrected step σ'2 in orange, followed by σ'3. Dashed arrows lead to two bottom boxes, Correction-Based SFT and RL Training, which show short-horizon rollouts from the verified prefix. Orange text highlights key benefits.
caption: Comparison between imitation-based distillation and our SCoRe framework. (a) Prior methods clone entire teacher trajectories. (b) Our approach lets the student explore independently; upon completion, the teacher reviews the full trajectory and minimally intervenes by correcting only the earliest error. Correction-based SFT mitigates the compounding errors of pure imitation. RL rollouts then start from this verified prefix, improving stability and efficiency.
abstract: Large Language Model agents achieve strong performance on multi-step reasoning and tool-use tasks, but their impressive capabilities typically rely on extremely large backbones. Existing distillation approaches train smaller students to imitate full teacher trajectories, yet reasoning and knowledge gaps between the teacher and student can cause compounding errors. We propose SCoRe, a student-centered framework in which the student generates training trajectories and the teacher corrects only the earliest error, producing training data matched to the student's abilities and exposing specific weaknesses. The student is first fine-tuned on corrected trajectories. Subsequently, short-horizon reinforcement learning starts from the verified prefix preceding the earliest error, with target rewards assigned at that step. This design enables the student to solve problems through unconstrained RL exploration rather than teacher imitation, while the short-horizon setup improves training stability. On 12 challenging benchmarks, a 7B-parameter student distilled with SCoRe closes the agentic performance gap with a 72B-parameter teacher.
